title: Seeing Neurons: Golgi, Cajal and the Neuron Doctrine

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: What does the neuron doctrine say about neuronal boundaries and communication?
cards.back: Neurons are separate cells, each bounded by its own membrane, that pass signals across specialized contacts.
cards.quote: Neurons are separate cells, each bounded by its own membrane, and they pass signals across specialized contacts.
cards.section: Touch or fusion: a question about 20 nanometres

cards.front: The theory that fine neuronal branches fuse into one continuous net is the {{c1::reticular theory}}.
cards.quote: The reticular theory said the fine branches fuse into one continuous net.
cards.section: Touch or fusion: a question about 20 nanometres

cards.front: How does signal transfer differ between chemical and electrical synapses?
cards.back: At a chemical synapse, one cell releases a messenger that acts on the next. At an electrical synapse, current passes through channels joining the cells.
cards.quote: at an electrical synapse, current passes straight through channels joining the two cells.
cards.section: Touch or fusion: a question about 20 nanometres

cards.front: A chemical synaptic cleft is about 20 nm wide; a light microscope resolves separations of about 200 nm. What fraction of the resolution limit is the cleft width, and is the gap resolvable?
cards.back: 20 nm / 200 nm = 0.1 = 10%. The cleft is about one-tenth of the resolution limit, so the gap is unresolved.
cards.quote: A gap of about 20 nanometres sits inside a blur about 200 nanometres across
cards.section: Touch or fusion: a question about 20 nanometres

cards.front: Two neuronal branches at different depths appear to join in a thick light-microscope section. If both neurons remain separate, what can the image still look like, and why?
cards.back: It can still look like one continuous line. Branches close together in depth can overlap in the image; apparent continuity does not establish fusion.
cards.quote: two branches that lie close together in depth, one above the other, can look like one line as you focus through them.
cards.section: Touch or fusion: a question about 20 nanometres

cards.front: In vertebrate development, why must neurons find partners, and how can they compete independently for a target's limited factor? Connect both consequences to the neuron doctrine.
cards.back: The rule is that neurons retain separate membrane-bounded compartments. Each must grow branches toward appropriate partners; where cells depend on a limited target factor, each cell can win or lose its own share.
cards.quote: In vertebrates, development has to wire separate cells together, each growing its branches toward the right partners.
cards.section: Touch or fusion: a question about 20 nanometres

cards.front: A large tracer remains in a neuron's soma but has not reached its distant branches. Does its failure to enter neighbours establish separate compartments at those distant contacts? What should be checked next?
cards.back: No. The rule requires testing what crosses the contact: the tracer must reach it first. Confirm filling of the branches and examine their contacts by electron microscopy for separate membranes.
cards.quote: Evidence that bears directly on the membrane at a contact, by imaging it or by testing what crosses it, can settle the question.
cards.section: Touch or fusion: a question about 20 nanometres

cards.front: Filling only a few cells completely, apparently at random, is called {{c1::sparse labelling}}.
cards.quote: This is sparse labelling: a few cells, filled completely, apparently at random.
cards.section: To see one cell, stain almost none

cards.front: Why can Nissl staining reveal cell layers but fail to answer whether neuronal branches fuse?
cards.back: It marks cell bodies and nuclei well, but leaves axons and dendrites almost invisible. The relevant contacts are on those fine processes.
cards.quote: axons and dendrites, the long thin processes where the question of fusion lives, stay almost invisible.
cards.section: To see one cell, stain almost none

cards.front: Why does filling a few neurons completely make their branching shapes easier to trace than staining every neuron?
cards.back: Most surrounding cells remain pale, so each filled neuron stands out rather than disappearing in a tangle of stained branches.
cards.quote: Most cells stay pale. A few fill with a black deposit from cell body to the finest twig
cards.section: To see one cell, stain almost none

cards.front: In an illustrative sparse stain, each neuron stains independently with probability 1/20. What is the probability both partners at a contact stain, and the probability the partner stains given one is stained?
cards.back: Both: (1/20) × (1/20) = 1/400 = 0.25%. Given one stained cell: 1/20 = 5%, by independence. These are illustrative probabilities, not measured staining rates.
cards.quote: As an illustration, not a measured rate, suppose cells take the stain independently and 1 cell in 20 is stained.
cards.section: To see one cell, stain almost none

cards.front: A researcher reduces the fraction of neurons stained to simplify an image. What happens to the ability to distinguish contact from fusion, and why?
cards.back: It does not solve the problem: both partners are even less likely to stain, and fewer stained cells do not improve optical resolution.
cards.quote: Resolution does not depend on how many cells are stained.
cards.section: To see one cell, stain almost none

cards.front: One Golgi-stained neuron is black throughout its visible branches while its neighbours remain pale. Does selective filling establish that its cytoplasm is separate?
cards.back: No. It hints at separateness, but unknown stain uptake could leave a fused region pale. Selective staining does not resolve the membrane at a contact.
cards.quote: Where only one side is stained, the pale partner could be a separate cell the stain missed or a fused part the stain did not reach.
cards.section: To see one cell, stain almost none

cards.front: Why could Golgi interpret silver-stained branches as a net while Cajal interpreted similar preparations as separate cells?
cards.back: Contacts remained unresolved. Golgi interpreted the tangle as continuity; Cajal emphasized repeatedly observed free endings. Each interpretation extended beyond what the contact image could show.
cards.quote: Each camp filled that blind spot with what its theory predicted.
cards.section: One slide, two readings

cards.front: His called the single young cell from which a nerve fibre grows a {{c1::neuroblast}}.
cards.quote: His argued that each nerve fibre grows out from a single cell, which he called a neuroblast.
cards.section: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells

cards.front: Why does young nervous tissue make a whole neuron easier to follow than adult tissue?
cards.back: It has fewer cells, shorter branches and little myelin to block staining, so a whole cell can fit in a section.
cards.quote: fewer cells, shorter branches, and little myelin, the fatty sheath that wraps many mature axons and can block the stain.
cards.section: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells

cards.front: Why does a nerve fibre growing from one cell support cellular independence without proving it?
cards.back: It establishes a separate cellular origin, but the fibre could still fuse with another cell at its far end.
cards.quote: Outgrowth shows where a fibre begins, not how it ends.
cards.section: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells

cards.front: In an embryo neural-tube culture, an observer watches a living nerve fibre extend out of the tissue. Which developmental claim does this support, and which contact question remains open?
cards.back: It supports fibre formation by outgrowth rather than merely inferring growth from fixed shapes. It does not show whether the fibre later fuses at its endpoint.
cards.quote: watched living nerve fibres grow out of them, the subject of the lesson on the growth cone.
cards.section: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells

cards.front: What is a growth cone in Cajal's description of a developing axon?
cards.back: A swelling at the tip of a young axon, interpreted as its advancing end, with the fibre lengthening behind it.
cards.quote: He named the structure the growth cone and read it as the advancing end of a fibre that lengthens behind it.
cards.section: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells

cards.front: Why was movement of Cajal's growth cones an inference rather than a direct observation?
cards.back: His specimens were fixed and dead. He inferred an advancing tip from a series of still shapes.
cards.quote: Every one of his specimens was fixed and dead, so the motion was an inference from a series of still shapes.
cards.section: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells

cards.front: By Cajal's law of dynamic polarization, a signal enters through dendrites and cell body and leaves through the {{c1::axon}}.
cards.back: A useful generalization with exceptions.
cards.quote: By the law of dynamic polarization, a signal enters a neuron through its dendrites and cell body and leaves through its axon.
cards.section: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells

cards.front: A receptor drives neuron A's dendrites; A's axon contacts neuron B's dendrites. Under dynamic polarization, where does the signal leave B, and why?
cards.back: Through B's axon. The rule assigns dendrites and cell body a receiving role and the axon a sending role; it is a generalization with exceptions.
cards.quote: In a chain, each cell has a receiving end and a sending end, so the order of the cells sets a direction
cards.section: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells

cards.front: Why does one-way signalling favour a chain of polarized cells without excluding a continuous net?
cards.back: A chain with receiving and sending ends explains direction, but a net could also contain polarized parts. Signal direction does not establish membrane separation.
cards.quote: continuity alone sets none, though a net could still have polarized parts.
cards.section: Evidence from development: fibres grow out of single cells

cards.front: At a chemical synapse, what membrane arrangement directly indicates two separate cells?
cards.back: Two membranes face each other across a cleft, and each cell's cytoplasm stops at its own membrane.
cards.quote: If the cells are separate, two membranes face each other across a gap, and each cell's cytoplasm stops at its own membrane.
cards.section: The direct test: look at the membrane

cards.front: An image resolves a neuronal junction: no membrane crosses it, and cytoplasm continues through it within a common outer boundary. Which interpretation does that junction support?
cards.back: Fusion at that junction. The decisive feature is continuous cytoplasm rather than two cytoplasms ending at facing membranes.
cards.quote: no membrane crosses the junction, and the cytoplasm carries on through it.
cards.section: The direct test: look at the membrane

cards.front: Why did electron microscopy of chemical synapses settle a question that light-microscope images of contacts could not?
cards.back: It resolved the two membranes and intervening cleft directly. Light microscopy could not distinguish separate membranes from a fused junction.
cards.quote: The electron microscope replaced the blur with two membranes, and the question was settled.
cards.section: The direct test: look at the membrane

cards.front: Channels crossing both neuronal membranes at an electrical synapse are called {{c1::gap junctions}}.
cards.quote: At an electrical synapse, the two membranes come within a few nanometres of each other, and channels called gap junctions cross both.
cards.section: A pore is not a fusion

cards.front: How do the two cells contribute to a gap-junction channel?
cards.back: Each supplies a protein ring called a hemichannel; the two halves dock across the gap.
cards.quote: Each cell supplies half of each channel, a ring of proteins called a hemichannel, and the two halves dock across the gap.
cards.section: A pore is not a fusion

cards.front: Why does direct passage of ions between electrically coupled neurons not make them one fused cell?
cards.back: Each cell retains its membrane. Transfer occurs through size-limited channels that can close, rather than through an unrestricted cytoplasmic bridge.
cards.quote: Each cell keeps its own membrane, and the channels can close.
cards.section: A pore is not a fusion

cards.front: What is a syncytium?
cards.back: A single cell with many nuclei sharing one cytoplasm.
cards.quote: a single cell with many nuclei sharing one cytoplasm
cards.section: A pore is not a fusion

cards.front: A 10-kilodalton dextran is injected into a vertebrate neuron coupled to neighbours by gap junctions. What happens to its distribution, and why?
cards.back: It stays in the injected cell. It is too large for those gap-junction channels; electrical coupling does not provide unrestricted cytoplasmic continuity.
cards.quote: A 10-kilodalton dextran, nearly 5 nanometres across, stays in the injected cell.
cards.section: A pore is not a fusion

cards.front: Neither a small tracer nor a large tracer leaves an injected neuron. Without first establishing that the small tracer passes the local gap junctions, can you conclude that the neuron lacks electrical coupling?
cards.back: No. The rule is that tracer permeability depends on the channel and molecule. A negative result with an unvalidated small tracer cannot exclude coupling; use a small tracer known to pass those junctions.
cards.quote: what passes depends on the connexin and the molecule
cards.section: A pore is not a fusion

cards.front: After a neuron is injected with two tracers, a small tracer reaches neighbours while a large tracer stays. Blocking intercellular channels prevents the small tracer's spread. What arrangement is supported?
cards.back: Separate compartments joined by size-limited channels. Selective transfer and its loss with channel blockade support regulated coupling rather than unrestricted fusion.
cards.quote: The small tracer is the control: it may reach a few coupled neighbours, and a connexin blocker should stop that.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: After one axon is cut, its detached segment degenerates while its cell-body-connected segment and neighbouring uncut axons survive. What dependence does this support?
cards.back: The fibre depends on its own cell body: degeneration follows loss of that connection rather than mere proximity to an injured axon.
cards.quote: each cell body and its fibres behaving as one unit.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An isolated cut axon degenerates, and a researcher concludes that neurons cannot fuse at contacts in grey matter. Why does the conclusion exceed the evidence?
cards.back: The rule is that evidence must test the contact in question. Both theories allowed separate neighbouring nerve fibres; degeneration there does not inspect grey-matter contacts. Damage can also cross between separate neurons.
cards.quote: No reticularist claimed that neighbouring fibres in a nerve were fused, so a single cut fibre could not tell the theories apart
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Design a test of neuronal separateness that combines tracer transfer with direct inspection of chemical contacts. State what each readout contributes.
cards.back: Fill a neuron with a large dextran and a small tracer known to pass local gap junctions; test small-tracer transfer with channel blockade. Then inspect its chemical contacts by electron microscopy. Size-selective transfer tests compartments; two facing membranes confirm structure. The rule is contact-level evidence.
cards.quote: A large dye that stays in one cell is strong evidence of a separate compartment, and the micrographs confirm it.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why does a positively charged Nissl dye concentrate in neuronal cell bodies?
cards.back: It binds negatively charged RNA and DNA. Cell bodies contain abundant ribosome-rich membranes, concentrating the stain there.
cards.quote: A Nissl dye such as cresyl violet carries a positive charge, so it sticks to negatively charged RNA and DNA.
cards.section: Stain chemistry

cards.front: Which neuronal branches formed Golgi's proposed reticulum, and how did he interpret dendrites?
cards.back: He proposed a network of fine axon branches. Dendrites appeared to end freely, and he thought they mainly served nutrition.
cards.quote: In Golgi's preparations dendrites seemed to end freely, and he thought they mainly served nutrition.
cards.section: Gerlach, Golgi and the changing reticulum

cards.front: A dendrite sends a signal to another dendrite across a contact with two separate membranes. Which claim needs an exception: dynamic polarization or neuronal separateness? Explain using both rules.
cards.back: The usual polarization rule needs an exception because dendrites can send at that contact. Neuronal separateness remains supported by the two membranes: direction of signalling and membrane boundaries are different tests.
cards.quote: The olfactory bulb, one of Cajal's own examples of polarized cells, was later found to have synapses from one dendrite onto another.
cards.section: Exceptions to one-way flow

cards.front: What feature of the squid's giant axon is a genuine exception to neuronal separateness?
cards.back: Axons from many cells fuse, so many cell bodies share one axonal cytoplasm.
cards.quote: many cell bodies share one axonal cytoplasm
cards.section: When neurons do fuse
